summary: One hidden-failure issue: `_manifests` silently skips a manifest it found at HEAD but failed to read via `git show`, without naming it — degrading the review's context with no surfacing, in contrast to `_changed_files` which explicitly lists what it could not include.

findings.title: `_manifests` silently drops a manifest it found but could not read at HEAD
findings.claim: In `_manifests`, candidates are discovered via `git ls-tree -r --name-only HEAD`, then each is read with `git show HEAD:<rel>` using `check=False`. If `returncode != 0`, the code does `continue` — the manifest is silently dropped from the payload with no accounting. The reviewer cannot distinguish 'a manifest exists at HEAD but was unreadable' from 'no manifest exists at HEAD', which is exactly the class of silent omission AC-4 was written to prevent. This is the same function that goes to lengths to state absence explicitly and name untracked manifests — but a found-and-then-unreadable manifest vanishes without a trace. The asymmetry is visible one function up: `_changed_files` appends every unreadable file to a `skipped` list and emits a 'NOT INCLUDED' section so the reviewer knows what it has not seen. `_manifests` has no equivalent. If `git show HEAD:<rel>` fails (encoding issue, git internal error, a submodules-related edge case), the review proceeds in a degraded state — missing a manifest the reviewer was never told existed.
findings.suggestion: Collect unreadable candidates into a `skipped` list and append a 'NOT INCLUDED (found at HEAD but unreadable)' section to the output, mirroring `_changed_files`. This keeps the invariant the function already aims for: the reviewer always knows what it has not seen.
